extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and policymakers debating the proposed U.S. Constitution (specifically the people of New York and legislators, 1787–1788)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and argumentative criteria for how a constitution should allocate authority and limits concerning military establishments, militia, and the means of national defense; intended to inform ratification debate and legislative design.

rubrics_metrics.name: National provision of common defense
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The means of guarding against it ought, in like manner, to be the objects of common councils and of a common treasury.' — Defense ought to be provided at the national (union) level rather than left to individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: dangers (in varying degrees) are common to all States; concentrating defensive establishments nationally is more equitable and secure than making border States sustain entire burden. Anti-pattern: leaving protection to isolated State provisions which produces inequality and insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: States should not separately maintain full military establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate and independent possession of military forces by States would be 'neither equitable as it respected [an exposed State] nor safe as it respected the other States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/risks: State-controlled forces would produce mutual jealousy, arms races, counterpoises, and could become 'engines for the abridgment or demolition of the national authority.' Example: powerful States might amass forces provoking others to seek counterweights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing Confederation prohibition on State ships/troops without Congress consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Articles of Confederation the States were expressly prohibited from having ships or troops unless with the consent of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/legal context: cited as precedent showing recognition of danger from separate State militaries; supports centralizing military authority under federal supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impracticable restraints on national legislature's discretion regarding defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions that unduly restrain the national legislature's discretion in providing for defense are improper because they either lack precise signification or are ineffectual when necessity arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: a prohibition that only forbids 'keeping up' armies but not 'raising' them is ambiguous ('What shall be denominated “keeping them up”?' ). Résumé: do not fetter legislative judgment with restrictions that cannot be observed in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on 'keeping standing armies in time of peace' is ambiguous and ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prohibition is confined to 'keeping them up' rather than also to 'raising' them, it has no precise signification and will be ineffectual; it's unclear how long is 'keeping up' or who judges the continuance of danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical problem: temporal/definitional vagueness invites circumvention. Anti-pattern: numeric/time limits without clear enforcement would allow evasion by executive/legislative discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit appropriations for maintaining an army to two years (periodic legislative review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's provision to limit appropriations for the support of an army to the period of two years steers clear of extremes while ensuring regular legislative reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: obliges legislature at least biennially to deliberate, forces public debate, enables opposition and State legislatures to sound alarms; practical restraint rather than absolute prohibition. Scoring note: valued as a salutary and powerful operation compared to ambiguous bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial deliberation as democratic check on military permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring re-appropriation at least every two years makes military support a recurrent matter of public debate and accountability ('The legislature...once at least in every two years, to deliberate upon the propriety of keeping a military force on foot').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: frequent votes attract public attention and opposition scrutiny; State legislatures act as vigilant guardians. Anti-pattern: permanent executive funds would evade this check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia cannot be relied upon alone for successful operations against a regular army
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The steady operations of war against a regular and disciplined army can only be successfully conducted by a force of the same kind.' — experience shows militia alone would likely have failed to secure independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Revolutionary War experience; militias valuable but lack the science acquired by diligence, perseverance, and practice. Policy implication: maintain some regular forces; consider economy and stability benefits of trained troops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute prohibition on raising armies in peacetime is impractical and unsafe
rubrics_metrics.description: To prohibit the RAISING of armies in time of peace would incapacitate the nation from preparing for defense before invasion—'We must receive the blow, before we could even prepare to return it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicality: dangers often are impending rather than actual; prevention and preparation (anticipatory policy) are legitimate. Anti-pattern: rigid constitutional bans that prevent necessary pre-emptive defense measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of executive-legislative combination does not justify impractical restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection that executive and legislative combination might usurp liberties is acknowledged but rejected as insufficient to support impracticable restrictions on defense powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument: conspiracies require time, secrecy, and perseverance unlikely in a system with biennial elections, party opposition, and public scrutiny; false positives should not undermine necessary powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies are more dangerous when possessed by those of whom the people are least suspicious
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As far as an army may be considered as a dangerous weapon of power, it had better be in those hands of which the people are most likely to be jealous than in those of which they are least likely to be jealous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: if danger exists, place coercive means under institutional actors who are under public suspicion and control (i.e., legislative oversight), not under seemingly benign but unchecked authorities. Consider popular oversight and accountability structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints that cannot be observed erode reverence for the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions that cannot be observed because public necessity will override them ('...how unequal parchment provisions are to a struggle with public necessity') weaken respect for fundamental law and set precedents for future breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: avoid embedding absolute constraints that will be readily violated; prefer working checks (e.g., periodic appropriations) that remain operative and maintain constitutional reverence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of federal authority to individuals aids peaceful enforcement without force
rubrics_metrics.description: Making federal authority operate directly upon individual citizens enables using ordinary magistrates in each State to execute federal laws, diminishing the need for force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: federal laws become 'the supreme law of the land' and state officers are bound to enforce them; consequence: broader jurisdictional reach reduces occasions for coercive enforcement by separate national armies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity of national government through ordinary operations reduces need for coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The more the operations of the national authority are intermingled in the ordinary exercise of government...the greater will be the probability that it will conciliate the respect and attachment of the community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: extend federal action to internal matters prudently to build accustomed legitimacy and thereby lessen reliance on force. Anti-pattern: a distant government 'continually at a distance and out of sight' breeds resistance and necessitates coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force in emergencies must be proportioned to the mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions that 'there may happen cases' where national government must resort to force (seditions, insurrections) and that 'the means to be employed must be proportioned to the extent of the mischief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: use militia for limited local commotions; raise regular forces when insurrection pervades a large area. Example: Massachusetts and Pennsylvania raised troops to quell disorders; policy should allow similar measures when necessary.
